---
title: The Workspace
llms-description: "What a Steward workspace contains, which files are authored and which are generated, what is durable and what is safe to delete, the journal, and how init handles version control."
---

## Overview

``` bash
steward init my-sweep
```

The deliverable of `init` is a **directory** — one that you and an agent
co-inhabit, and that a third party can pick up cold. That framing does real
work: it means everything important has to be written down rather than held in
somebody's session.

``` text
my-sweep/
  AGENTS.md          # authored  — bootstrap: "you are tending a run; read the runbook"
  CLAUDE.md          # authored  — symlink to AGENTS.md
  _steward.md         # authored  — your standing rules
  evalset.py          # authored  — your definition (or flow.yaml / hawk.yaml)
  .env                # authored  — credentials, if you keep them here

  journal.jsonl       # DURABLE   — append-only record; the source of truth
  status.md           # generated — rewritten by every tend
  steward.log         # generated — whether Steward's own machinery worked

  logs/               # DURABLE   — the flat log directory: the CURRENT definition's results
  logs-archive/       # DURABLE   — superseded, removed, and failed logs; never deleted

  .steward/           # DISPOSABLE — claim, manifest, in-flight record, caches
```

`init` **only ever creates.** Everything authored in a workspace is somebody's
work, so a second run reports each path as created or kept rather than restoring
a pristine copy over it. `.gitignore` is the single exception and gains missing
entries idempotently, because those entries are Steward's rather than yours.

## Four categories, and only one is safe to delete

The obvious split — human-readable at the top, machine-owned in `.steward/` —
conflates *who writes a file* with *whether it can be recovered*. The categories
that matter are:

| category | files | if you delete it |
|----|----|----|
| **authored** | `_steward.md`, `AGENTS.md`, the definition | your own work is gone |
| **durable machine state** | `journal.jsonl`, `logs/`, `logs-archive/` | the audit trail, or the results, are gone |
| **authored by the agent** | `scanning.md`, `analysis.md` *(not yet implemented)* | the investigation is gone, and re-runs from scratch |
| **disposable** | everything in `.steward/`, `status.md`, `steward.log` | rebuilt on the next turn, or simply gone with no loss |

Note that gitignored is **not** the same category as disposable. `logs/` and
`logs-archive/` are ignored by git because `.eval` files are large outputs shared
through a log store rather than through source control — they are still durable.
Only `.steward/` is safe to remove.

## The journal

`journal.jsonl` is the append-only record of what was observed and what was
decided. It is the one file in the directory that **nothing else can
reconstruct**, which is why it sits at the top level beside the authored files
rather than in `.steward/`.

It is also what marks a directory as a workspace, and it is the only file that
could. `.steward/` is disposable so its absence proves nothing; a definition can
sit in any directory; `_steward.md` is optional. So `init` opens the journal with
a real `initialized` event, and the account of what happened starts where the
workspace does.

Every event shares a UTC timestamp and a type. Today a turn appends what it
observed — task states, whether the definition has drifted, the verdict, the
open item ids, and the concurrency settings in force — and `steward ack` appends
an acknowledgment. More event types arrive with the features that produce them.

Two properties are deliberate:

-   **Damage costs one line, never the file.** A torn write from a crash loses
    the last event; everything before it reads normally.
-   **An unrecognised event type is data, not an error.** A workspace outlives
    the Steward that wrote it, so a reader yields an unknown type as a generic
    event rather than refusing the file.

There is no rendered `journal.md` and no `steward journal` command. Append-only
JSONL diffs cleanly in git — every commit is pure additions — and
`jq -r '.type' journal.jsonl` serves a reader with no Steward installed.

### `status.md` vs `steward.log`

Two generated files, and the rule dividing them is one question:

> Is this a fact about **the eval set**, or about **Steward**?

`status.md` and the journal answer the first. A tend that crashed, a spawn that
failed, an unreadable `_steward.md` — those are facts about the runner, and they
go to `steward.log`, which is bounded and disposable.

The split answers something neither could alone: *"no tend for four hours"* is
computable from the journal's silence, and *why* is in `steward.log`. Had they
shared a file, a run whose tends were crashing would look like a run with
nothing to report.

## Losing `.steward/`

It mostly fails in the safe direction, and it is worth knowing exactly how much:

-   The manifest is re-captured from the definition by the next `launch`.
-   In-flight records are rebuilt by sweeping the process table.
-   **Running workers survive.** Each carries its own identity in its
    environment, so the next turn still sees them and schedules nothing over
    them.
-   What is actually lost is provenance and a re-capture.

Two cases are not safe, and they take the same rule:

-   **A worker mid-startup dies.** Before it reaches `eval_set()` it has not yet
    read its instructions, so deleting them kills it. That is the right outcome
    — a dead worker is respawned once, from nothing — and what is lost is a few
    seconds of imports.
-   **Deleting the claim file by hand is worse than useless.** The lock lives in
    the kernel, attached to the inode, so unlinking the file leaves the holder
    holding it and lets the next tend create a fresh file, lock *that*, and run
    concurrently. Nothing can detect that from the new file's side.

> **So: delete `.steward/` when nothing is running, not as a reflex.**

There is deliberately no `steward unclaim`. The usual reason to want one does not
arise: the claim is held only for the seconds a turn runs, a tend that died
released it on the way out whether it meant to or not, and one that is wedged is
killed by the turn that finds it.

## Version control

`init` runs `git init` **if, and only if, there is no repository already**.
Detection walks up from the directory, because a workspace created inside an
existing project — `evals/sweep-2026-08/` in a monorepo — belongs to that
repository, and initialising a nested one there is a footgun rather than a
convenience. It announces what it did, and `--no-git` is there for people who
mean it.

Either way it writes a **local** `.gitignore` listing `.steward/`, `logs/`, and
`logs-archive/`. Scoping the rules to a nested file means Steward never edits
one it does not own — your parent project's ignore rules stay untouched.

A missing git is an ordinary condition rather than an error. Some runs happen on
machines with no git and no network, where an object store is the only channel
out.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Committing an append-only journal gives a second, independent record of when
each decision was made — git's own metadata — and any edit to a past entry shows
up in review as a *modification* rather than an append. It does not make the
record tamper-proof, but it makes tampering visible in ordinary review.
:::

One caveat if you ever read log provenance: a workspace that `init` made its own
repository has Steward writing `journal.jsonl` and `status.md` into that tree as
it runs, so every log is marked as coming from a dirty tree. That flag means "a
run touched this tree", not "the source was edited", and it should not be built
on.
